segments: The tenth dynasty.
The Arab kings.
Finally, he was coming with four thousand [men],
the Bulgarians, whom Leo had hired, came upon him
and killed many of his [men].
And with difficulty Maslama escaped and reached the great camp,
which was entrenched on the western side of Constantinople opposite the Golden Gate.
And he made an entrenchment {OCR?} in front of them between the camp and the city,
and a ditch behind them facing the Bulgarians.
Now on the right and on the left was the sea.
And the Arabs were attacked by the people of the city and by the Bulgarians,
and at sea by the ships of the Romans.
And in fewer than two thousand, they were not able to go out to bring provisions for themselves, that is, the Arabs.
And the Arabs were in distress from the outside more than the Byzantines {lit. Turks} on the inside.
And winter and famine overtook them,
as well as the Bulgarians who were killing them.
And to this extent the Arabs were distressed by famine,
that they chewed the pitch of the ships.
And while Maslama was deceiving them,
saying, "Behold, gifts are coming for them from the king,"
news came of the death of King Sulayman.
[Umar] ibn Abd al-Aziz,
two years and five months.
This man sent to bring him news of the army that was against Constantinople.
And Maslama wrote deceitful letters,
saying, "The people are doing well,
and the city is close to being captured."
And when he learned the truth from the messenger,
he sent to him,
that he should take the army and leave.
He, however, made excuses because of the winter.
And when the severity of the winter had passed,
another messenger came, saying to the people:
"If Maslama does not consent,
they should leave on their own."
And at their departure,
the Romans killed many of them by sea and by land.
Then Umar sent them twenty thousand horses,
and to each man ten dinars for the expenses of their rescue.
And on account of the shame that befell the Arabs in their expedition against Constantinople,
great hatred arose in the heart of Umar against the Christians,
and he oppressed them greatly.
And he abolished their semantra {church bells},
and that they should not raise their voices in prayer,
and should not wear soldiers' clothing,
and should not ride on a saddle.
And in the year one thousand and thirty-four
